summary: An informational memo describing the issues and requirements of QoS-based routing and proposing a framework for it in the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo asks how Internet routing could take the needs of a traffic flow into account, instead of always sending it down the shortest path. It says each network should be free to design its own routing inside its borders, while the information passed between networks stays small and simple. It also lists what a network must be able to do for that to count as quality-of-service routing.

subtitle: A framework for choosing network paths by what the network can actually carry, not only by which path is shortest.

tldr.problem: Internet routing optimises for connectivity alone: it sends traffic along one shortest path, moves it whenever a better path appears, and has no way to use a second path when the first is full. That is not enough for flows that need a guaranteed level of service.
tldr.mechanism: The memo keeps the traditional split between routing inside one network and routing between networks. Each network may run its own QoS-based scheme, while the exchange between networks stays small: border routers advertise the QoS engineered for transit traffic, and traffic is bundled into aggregated streams.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational. It describes the issues, sets out broad requirements for intradomain routing, and sketches an interdomain model, but it does not specify the interdomain mechanism itself.

today: RFC 2386 is an Informational memo from August 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines no protocol and sets no standard: it argues for an approach to QoS-based routing and leaves the interdomain mechanism itself as the next step in the evolution of wide-area, multidomain QoS-based routing.

sections.title: A Two-Pronged Approach to QoS Routing
sections.content:
RFC 2386 proposes a framework for QoS-based routing in the Internet, and explains why the authors think the problem should be attacked from two directions at once. The first is to encourage the growth of new intradomain routing architectures, so that autonomous systems of any size can develop solutions suited to their own needs. The second is to keep the interactions between those autonomous systems simple, consistent and stable.

The split follows the traditional separation between intradomain and interdomain routing. A scheme such as QOSPF or Integrated PNNI can be deployed inside an autonomous system without restriction, as long as it can talk to the others through one common interdomain routing protocol. The authors argue that this removes the need for a single all-encompassing solution to a problem about which there are many different views, and it lets several ideas be developed and deployed at the same time while agreement on the interdomain architecture is still being worked out. They also argue that the eventual success of a QoS-routed Internet depends on how easily it can evolve.

The memo is explicit about what it does not do. It does not specify the details of intradomain QoS-based routing architectures, and it does not specify the interface between reservation protocols such as RSVP and QoS-based routing. What it does do is describe the issues, state broad requirements on intradomain routing, and set out an extension of the current interdomain model that supports QoS.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not design one protocol. It argues that the inside of each network and the links between networks should be handled separately: each network can build whatever routing works for it, and the networks agree on one simple way of exchanging information. That keeps several designs in play at once and makes the change easier to roll out.

sections.title: What Today's Routing Does and Why It Falls Short
sections.content:
Internet routing today optimises for connectivity alone. The service offered is best-effort, and protocols such as OSPF and RIP use shortest path routing, optimised for a single arbitrary metric, administrative weight or hop count. They are also opportunistic: traffic moves to a new path as soon as a better one is found, even when the path in use could still carry the traffic. A path that is acceptable but not optimal cannot be used.

QoS-based routing has to extend this in three ways. First, several paths between node pairs must be calculated, and some service classes need extra routing metrics such as delay and available bandwidth. If those metrics change often, routing updates become more frequent and consume network bandwidth and router CPU cycles. Second, opportunistic behaviour becomes a problem: if route calculation is tied to resources that get consumed, such as available bandwidth, traffic shifts more often, routing oscillations appear as traffic moves back and forth, and the delay and jitter seen by users vary more. Third, when the best path cannot admit a new flow, that traffic cannot be forwarded even if an adequate alternative path exists, because today's optimal path algorithms do not support alternate routing.

QoS-based routing is not the same as resource reservation, and the memo separates the two. Reservation protocols such as RSVP provide a way to request and reserve network resources, but they do not provide a mechanism for finding a path that has enough resources to meet the request. QoS-based routing can find such a path, with a good chance of accommodating the flow, but it does not reserve anything. The two are therefore used together. A simple form already exists in Type of Service (TOS) routing: in OSPF a different shortest-path tree can be computed for each of the 8 TOS values in the IP header, which separates whole classes of traffic over multiple routes without assuring that resources are not overbooked along the path.

The objectives of QoS-based routing are to find a feasible path from among several choices, subject to policy constraints such as path cost and provider selection; to make better use of network resources and improve total throughput; and to degrade gracefully when the engineered capacity is temporarily short, which a state-insensitive routing scheme cannot do.
sections.plainLanguage: Today's routers send traffic along the single shortest path and move it whenever a better one appears, even when the path in use is fine. Routing that takes quality of service into account has to compute several candidate paths, keep them from flapping as load changes, and be able to send traffic down a second path when the first is full. Choosing a path is still not the same as reserving capacity; the two are used together.

sections.title: Minimum Requirements for Intradomain Routing
sections.content:
Section 4 lists the minimum requirements a scheme must meet to count as QoS-based routing inside an autonomous system. The requirements are deliberately broad so that different approaches can qualify.

  • The scheme must route a flow along a path that can accommodate its QoS requirements, or indicate that the flow cannot be admitted with the QoS currently being requested.
  • It must indicate disruptions to the current route of a flow due to topological changes.
  • It must accommodate best-effort flows without any resource reservation requirements, so that present best-effort applications and protocol stacks need not change to run in a domain employing QoS-based routing.
  • It may optionally support QoS-based multicasting with receiver heterogeneity and shared reservation styles.

Two further capabilities are recommended rather than required: capabilities to optimise resource usage, and implementation of higher level admission control procedures to limit the overall resource utilisation by individual flows. Higher level admission control is the process of deciding, from estimates and policy requirements for the overall resource usage of a flow, whether the flow setup should proceed at all. It can fail a flow that local admission control at each node would have accepted. The memo notes that fairness is a problem here, because flows with smaller reservations tend to be routed more successfully than flows with large reservations for a given engineered capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: To count as quality-of-service routing, a scheme has to meet four conditions: it must either find a path that can carry a flow's requirements or refuse the flow, it must report when a change breaks a route, it must carry ordinary best-effort traffic without changes to existing applications, and it may support multicast. Improving resource use and limiting the resources one flow can take are recommended rather than required.

sections.title: The Interdomain Routing Model
sections.content:
The interdomain model has one overriding requirement: scalability. Because of that, interdomain routing cannot be based on highly dynamic network state information. It has to be aided by sound network engineering and relatively sparse information exchange between independent routing domains. The memo's picture is a hierarchy. Autonomous systems exchange standardized routing information through border nodes, each autonomous system may itself consist of interconnected autonomous systems, and at the lowest level each autonomous system runs an intradomain QoS-based routing scheme, either proprietary or standardised by intradomain routing efforts such as QOSPF.

The information exchanged between domains has to enable six functions: determining reachability to various destinations, producing loop-free flow routes, address aggregation whenever possible, determining the QoS that will be supported on the path to a destination, optionally determining multiple paths for a destination based on service classes, and expressing routing policies including monetary cost as a function of flow parameters, usage and administrative factors. The first three are already part of existing interdomain routing and the fifth is a straightforward extension of it. The main problem areas are therefore the fourth, QoS, and the sixth, cost.

The memo's answer to the QoS problem is to avoid measuring what changes from moment to moment. Rather than compute paths from residual or instantaneous values of metrics, border routers advertise the QoS that has been engineered for aggregate transit flows, based on the traffic expected from each neighbouring autonomous system and the QoS needs that go with it. The metric therefore corresponds to the QoS capabilities of a virtual path engineered through the autonomous system, and a different metric may be used for a different neighbour. Excess traffic beyond the engineered limit may be handled as best effort or marked with a discard bit. Failures should trigger recomputation of path metrics; the arrival of flows within the engineered limit should not.

Two further mechanisms keep the amount of state manageable. Flow aggregation classifies transit traffic into a few aggregated streams rather than routing it at the individual flow level: an entry border router groups flows by egress node and QoS requirement, and the aggregated stream is routed inside the autonomous system as a single flow, while the entry border router tracks the resource requirements of each transit flow and applies admission control against the engineered limit. Path cost must keep a uniform meaning as it passes through intermediate domains. A domain may add a locally significant component while the value travels, but what the next domain receives must be the original intent plus the incremental cost of transiting the current domain, not the current domain's internal meaning. The memo also flags an unsolved problem: how to determine the cost when the QoS promised for a flow was not actually delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: Between networks, the exchange of information has to stay small, because too much detail does not scale. So a network advertises the quality of service it has engineered room for, not what its links happen to be doing right now. It also bundles many traffic flows into a few streams to limit the amount of state, and it has to keep the meaning of a price stable as the price travels from one network to the next.

sections.title: QoS-Based Multicast Routing
sections.content:
Multicast makes the problem harder, because IP multicast lets receivers join and leave at any time and lets each receiver ask for a different service. The memo lists the goals: scalability to large groups with dynamic membership, robustness in the presence of topological changes, support for receiver-initiated heterogeneous reservations, support for shared reservation styles, and support for global admission control, meaning administrative control of the resources consumed by the multicast flow.

Two models are compared. Under multicast source routing, the first-hop router computes the tree from the source's traffic advertisement. This blends well with the present RSVP signalling model and works well when receiver reservations are homogeneous and the same as the maximum reservation derived from the sender advertisement. Its disadvantages are the extra effort needed to accommodate heterogeneous reservations and the difficulty of optimising resource allocation for shared reservations.

Under a receiver-oriented model, sender traffic advertisements are multicast over a best-effort tree that can differ from the QoS-accommodating tree for the sender's data, receiver discovery overheads are minimised by using a scalable scheme such as PIM or CBT, each receiver-side router independently computes a QoS-accommodating path from the source based on that receiver's reservation, and routers aggregate the reservations from several receivers. The advantages are that heterogeneous reservations and shared reservations can be handled. The disadvantages are incompatibility with the present RSVP signalling model and a need to rely on reverse paths when link state routing is not used.

Two sources of overhead decide how well this scales: the cost of receiver discovery, and the cost of computing a QoS-accommodating path when flow-specific state has to be collected. Under the RSVP model, reservations are established on the path the sender traffic characterisation already used, so there is no path computation overhead; under the QOSPF model of multicast source routing, receiver location broadcasts add overhead and the need to track existing flow paths adds more. At the interdomain level, scalability can be achieved by computing QoS-based multicast paths independently in each domain, as the QOSPF multicast source routing scheme allows in separate OSPF areas. Multicast flows also need admission control: a router computing a path for a receiver must determine whether the incremental resource allocation for that receiver is excessive under an administratively determined admission control policy.
sections.plainLanguage: With multicast, each receiver can ask for a different level of service and can join or leave at any time, so choosing one path for everyone is not enough. One model computes the whole tree at the sender, which is simple but awkward when receivers want different things. Another computes a path separately for each receiver, which handles differences well but costs more. In both cases a router has to check that the extra resources a receiver asks for are within the limit the administrator set.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo's security section is short. Routing security in general is about maintaining the integrity of the routing protocol in the presence of unintentional or malicious introduction of information that may lead to protocol failure. QoS-based routing requires two additional measures: validating the QoS requests that flows make, and preventing resource-depletion threats, in which flows are allowed to make arbitrary resource requests along various paths in the network. Excessive resource consumption by an errant flow results in denial of resources to legitimate flows.

The memo says these situations may be prevented by setting up proper policy constraints, charging models and policing at various points in the network, but that the formalisation of such protection requires work.

The related work section reviews adaptive routing in circuit-switched networks, in ATM networks and in packet networks, covering the k-shortest-path scheme, trunk reservation, dynamic alternate routing, AT&T's Real-Time Network Routing scheme, the ATM Forum's PNNI protocol and Integrated PNNI, and the ARPANET's distance-vector scheme. Two findings recur. Alternate routing improves throughput when traffic load is relatively light but adversely affects performance when the load is heavy, because circuits are then routed along longer paths and use more capacity. And flooding state information is a reasonable choice with static link metrics but can impact performance adversely with dynamic metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing has to survive someone feeding it bad information on purpose. Quality-based routing adds two new risks: a flow asking for resources it will not use, and a flow taking capacity that other flows need. Policy, charging and policing can prevent both, but the memo says the rules for doing so had not yet been written down. Its review of older work finds that spreading traffic over several paths helps when a network is quiet and hurts when it is busy.
